title: Teaching Portfolio
text:
Teaching philosophy
My primary goal as an instructor is to make sure every student feels safe, welcome, and respected, and knows they belong in the mathematics classroom. Students arrive with very different experiences of mathematics, and some have had far more support and encouragement than others. I share the conviction behind Federico Ardila-Mantilla’s axioms for mathematics education: mathematical talent is distributed equally across groups of people, and every student deserves meaningful mathematical experiences and to be treated with dignity and respect.
My own interest in mathematics took time to develop. As a child I struggled with mathematics and physics, but I still vividly remember the experiments shown to us by a physics teacher who made a two-hour journey through Indian city traffic to teach our weekend classes. That teacher showed me how much an instructor can do by making room for curiosity and believing that students can understand. His example is why I volunteer with math circles and with science and mathematics camps for girls.

Students should do mathematics, not just watch it; they should do it together; and they should be cared for as whole people.
The three commitments that run through my teaching

title: Teaching Portfolio
text:
Principles in practice


1

Doing mathematics, not just watching it
After introducing a concept and working an example, I give students time to try a related problem before I present a solution. I circulate, offering small hints and asking questions that help them find a next step. When a student is unsure or makes a mistake, my first concern is to help them feel at ease: an incomplete idea is still worth discussing, and I openly acknowledge my own mistakes.



2

Finding the right picture
A good picture often makes sense before a formal statement does. In MTH 314, I used geometric transformations of the plane so that students understood what eigenvalues and eigenvectors tell us about a linear transformation while they learned to compute them.



3

Learning together
Explaining an idea to a classmate is one of the best ways to understand it, and asking a classmate is often easier than asking the instructor. I build group work into class time in person, and I design online courses so that live sessions are spent working together.



4

Caring for the whole student
My students have lives and pressures outside my course. I offer flexible deadlines in difficult circumstances, space exams so students have time to prepare, and avoid scheduling an exam right after a long weekend or break. An exam is a fair measure of learning only when students have had a fair chance to prepare.



5

Mistakes as a reason to keep working
Standards-based grading in MTH 103A gave students further opportunities to show mastery of topics they first found difficult, so an unsuccessful attempt became a reason to keep working rather than a final verdict.



6

Not waiting for students to come to me
In an online course a struggling student can easily go unnoticed. In MTH 314 I wrote to students who were not doing well and met with them individually on Zoom.









Using AI to sharpen proof reading. In MTH 317H recitations I give students poorly written AI-generated proofs and ask them to find unjustified assumptions, missing steps, and errors that are easy to overlook when an explanation sounds convincing, and to say what the AI did well. The aim is for students to understand its possibilities and limits, and to gain the confidence to assess an argument for themselves, not to have AI do their homework.

Teaching across course contexts


MTH 103A: College Algebra I
Instructor of record · Spring 2025 · about 60 students
Taught in an active-learning classroom in the MSU Union, with round tables and screens throughout the room. Students worked in groups while two undergraduate learning assistants and I circulated, and I wrote live on an iPad projected to every table. The class met daily at 8 a.m. through a Michigan winter, so I offered a Zoom option for icy mornings and possible closures. I wrote my own lecture notes and worksheets and used standards-based grading.


MTH 124: Survey of Calculus
Instructor of record · Summer 2023 · fully online
Structured as a flipped classroom. Students watched videos I recorded before class, meeting new ideas at their own pace, so live sessions could be spent working problems together and consolidating the theory. The course ran on Piazza with engagement points, and students could optionally make a short “reel” introducing themselves to help them find classmates to work with.


MTH 314: Matrix Algebra with Applications
Instructor of record · Summer 2024 · fully online
I wrote lecture notes in LaTeX and also shared the handwritten notes produced live in each Zoom lecture, so students had both a polished reference and a record of how each argument unfolded. I recorded lecture videos, posted short check-in videos between meetings, and designed in-class Python assignments so students practiced the computational side of matrix algebra alongside the theory.


MTH 317H: Honors Linear Algebra
Recitation leader · Fall 2026
I teach the proof techniques from MTH 299 that students need but may not yet know, with worksheets that ask why a concept is useful or needed. Complete solutions are released twenty-four hours after each deadline so students can check their reasoning. Course materials →


I have also been instructor of record for MTH 234: Multivariable Calculus (Fall 2024), and a teaching assistant for courses including MTH 299 (Introduction to Proofs) and MTH 818 (Graduate Algebra I). See the full list on the Teaching page.

title: Galois module structure of Deligne–Lusztig varieties for \mathbf{G} = \mathrm{GL}_3
text:
Summary
Deligne and Lusztig defined a finite étale cover Y(w) \to X(w) of varieties. It is attached to any connected reductive group \mathbf{G} defined over a finite field \mathbb{F}_q, with a Frobenius endomorphism F, and to a Weyl group element w \in W.
We consider the ramified Galois covers 
\overline{Y(w)} \longrightarrow \overline{X(w)}
 of the natural compactifications of these Deligne–Lusztig varieties. Our goal is to calculate the Lefschetz numbers for the action of the covering group on the coherent cohomology of the structure sheaf of \overline{Y(w)}. The covering group is \mathbf{T}^{wF}, the \mathbb{F}_p-points of a torus.
These numbers determine the representation of \mathbf{T}^{wF} on the alternating sum 
\sum_i (-1)^i \, H^i\big(\overline{Y(w)}, \mathcal{O}_{\overline{Y(w)}}\big).
 The paper gives these Lefschetz numbers explicitly for Deligne–Lusztig surfaces, in the cases \mathbf{G}^F = \mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{F}_p) and \mathbf{G}^F = \mathrm{U}_3(\mathbb{F}_p).

title: Galois module structure of Deligne–Lusztig varieties for \mathbf{G} = \mathrm{GL}_3
text:
Method
The approach is to work étale-locally to resolve the singularities of \overline{Y(w)}, and to construct a smooth model carrying an action of \mathbf{T}^{wF} that extends the action on \overline{Y(w)}. The local calculations lead to toric geometry. The Hirzebruch–Jung algorithm for minimal resolutions of toric surfaces then supplies what is needed to apply the Lefschetz–Riemann–Roch theorem. In both the split and the unitary case, the resulting Lefschetz numbers are explicit and nonzero.

title: Galois module structure of Deligne–Lusztig varieties for \mathbf{G} = \mathrm{GL}_3
text:
Background: geometric Galois module theory
Geometric Galois module theory studies how a finite group acting on an algebraic variety or scheme gives module structures on its cohomological and arithmetic invariants. If a finite group G acts on a variety X, then G acts naturally on cohomology groups such as H^i(X, \mathcal{F}). These groups can then be studied as modules over the group ring k[G], or over the corresponding integral group rings in arithmetic settings.
A central problem is to determine these module structures, and their equivariant Euler characteristics, for a Galois cover X \to X/G. This extends classical Galois module theory to higher dimensions. In the classical theory, one studies rings of integers in finite Galois extensions of local or global fields as modules over group rings.
The subject draws on arithmetic geometry, algebraic geometry, representation theory, and algebraic K-theory. Ramification and fixed-point data play a central role in the structure of the resulting Galois modules.

I am a fifth-year Ph.D. candidate in mathematics at Michigan State University, working with Prof. Georgios Pappas. I completed a B.S.–M.S. dual degree in mathematics at IISER Tirupati in 2022, where I worked with Prof. D. S. Nagaraj and wrote my master’s thesis on class field theory.
I am broadly interested in arithmetic geometry and representation theory, specifically finite group actions on algebraic varieties and the Galois module structure of their cohomology groups. Recently I have been working on Deligne–Lusztig varieties; see my preprint under preparation and the research page.
Outside mathematics, I enjoy Carnatic and Hindustani classical music, playing the bansuri (Indian bamboo flute), badminton, literature, and social justice advocacy.

text:
Projects

Arithmetic statistics of p-torsion in class groups of quartic number fields
2026–present
I’m a participant in Sameera Vemulapalli’s project group at Arithmetic Geometry at UNT 2 (University of North Texas, August 3–7, 2026). We study p-torsion in class groups of quartic number fields that admit an integral basis of the form 1, x, y, xy, in connection with Bhargava’s parametrizations of quartic rings.
Some Magma code and preliminary analysis are in the project repository.


Efficient computation of the Weil pairing for Drinfeld modules
2026–present
I’m a participant in Antoine Leudière’s project group at Rethinking Number Theory (online, June 22–July 3, 2026). We’re working toward explicit computation of Weil pairings for Drinfeld modules by implementing pairing algorithms in SageMath and other open-source software.


Who Bears the Congestion Price?
Erdős Institute Data Science Boot Camp, Summer 2026
On January 5, 2025, New York became the first US city to charge vehicles for entering a defined zone: the Manhattan Central Business District south of 60th Street. Using public TLC trip records (about 37M Yellow taxi trips and about 202M Uber/Lyft trips, February–June 2024 compared with the same months of 2025), we ask who bears this fee and whether it reduced trips.

The burden is uneven, and the finding is stable. A flat per-trip fee is a much larger share of short, low-cost trips, which are concentrated in the dense Manhattan core, than of long airport trips. The zone ranking stays stable across the tested denominator floors, giving a reusable, reproducible burden metric (DS_z).
The volume models show suggestive negative patterns. Three regression-with-controls designs compare burden, exposure, and vehicle groups. A 2023→2024 no-fee placebo and sensitivity checks limit a direct fee-caused interpretation.

title: MTH 317H: Honors Linear Algebra
text:
MTH 317H is an advanced introduction to linear algebra and abstract vector spaces, with a strong emphasis on mathematical communication. Students learn to construct logical arguments and write clear, rigorous proofs.
The course has two lecture sections that meet on Tuesdays and Thursdays and cover the linear algebra. I lead the Monday recitations. For roughly the first half of the semester, recitation is an accelerated introduction to proof writing (essentially the content of MTH 299), taught through notes and collaborative worksheets. Later recitations practice the linear algebra from lecture. Many recitations start with a short quiz.
Learning objectives

Understand and use key concepts of linear algebra: vector spaces, linear transformations, systems of linear equations, determinants, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
Gain proficiency in constructing and writing proofs.

Texts (all free online, except the last two)

Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed. (LADR)
Sergei Treil, Linear Algebra Done Wrong (LADW)
Richard Hammack, Book of Proof, 3rd ed.
Kevin Houston, How to Think Like a Mathematician
Chartrand, Polimeni and Zhang, Mathematical Proofs: A Transition to Advanced Mathematics
